function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that will give you a Docker image, a Kubernetes deployment/service, and a GitHub Actions workflow that builds the image and pushes it to a registry whenever you push to `main`.  
Feel free to copy the snippets into your repository and adjust any values (image tags, ports, secrets, etc.) to match your own environment.

---

## 1️⃣  Clone the repo

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣  Analyse & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Node 14 (slim variant)
FROM node:14-slim

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json (if present) first
# This allows Docker to cache the npm install step
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm install --production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port that the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official `node:14-slim` image – small, stable, and contains everything needed to run a Node.js app.  
> * Copies only the `package*.json` files first so that Docker can cache the `npm install` step.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`--production`) to keep the image lean.  
> * Exposes port `3000` – the port used by the sample `app.js` in the repo.  
> * Starts the app with `node app.js`.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a folder called `k8s` in the root of the repo and add a file named `deployment.yaml` inside it:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Creates a Deployment with 2 replicas of your Node.js app.  
> * Exposes port `3000` inside the pod.  
> * Creates a ClusterIP Service that forwards traffic from port `80` to the pod’s port `3000`.  
> * Replace `<YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>` with the registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`).

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `ci-cd.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑platform builder)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker registry
      - name: Log in to DockerHub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a kubeconfig secret)
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v1
        with:
          manifests: k8s/*.yaml
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Secrets you’ll need**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username.  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token or password.  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – a base64‑encoded kubeconfig file that points to the cluster where you want to deploy.  

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * Triggers on every push to `main`.  
> * Builds the Docker image and pushes it to your registry.  
> * Deploys the new image to Kubernetes using the manifests in `k8s/`.  

---

## 3️⃣  Commit & push the changes

```bash
# Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"

# Push to main
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, push it to your registry, and deploy it to Kubernetes.

---

## 4️⃣  Verify

1. **Check the Actions tab** – you should see a successful run.  
2. **Verify the image** – log into your registry and confirm that `nodejs-welcome:latest` exists.  
3. **Check the cluster** – run `kubectl get pods,svc -n <namespace>` to see the Deployment and Service.  

---

### 🎉 Done!

You now have a fully automated CI/CD pipeline that builds a Docker image from your Node.js app, pushes it to a registry, and deploys it to Kubernetes whenever you push to `main`. Adjust the image tags, registry, and secrets as needed for your environment. Happy coding!
